name: InfluxDB
license: MIT or Apache 2.0 (InfluxDB 3 Core); MIT (1.x and 2.x); InfluxDB 3 Enterprise and InfluxDB Cloud are proprietary
summary: The best-known time-series database, fed by line protocol and Telegraf; now in its third generation, a Rust rewrite that keeps data as Parquet files on object storage.
intro: InfluxDB stores measurements (tables) of timestamped points with tags and fields, written as line protocol over HTTP, usually by Telegraf or a client library. It exists in three incompatible generations: 1.x and 2.x are a Go server on InfluxData’s own Time-Structured Merge Tree (TSM) engine with a series index, and 3.x, the current one, is a Rust rewrite on Apache Arrow, DataFusion and Parquet. In InfluxDB 3 Core, one `influxdb3` process on port 8181 validates each write into memory, flushes a write-ahead log to object storage (S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob or local disk) every second, keeps recent data in a queryable buffer, and every ten minutes persists the oldest data as Parquet files. Queries use SQL or InfluxQL over HTTP or Arrow Flight SQL, helped by last-value and distinct-value caches, and an embedded Python processing engine runs plugins on new writes or on a schedule.

Core is free under MIT or Apache 2.0 but has no compactor: its Parquet files stay in small 10-minute blocks, and by default a query may read at most 432 of them, about 72 hours of data. InfluxDB 3 Enterprise, under a commercial licence priced by CPU cores, adds compaction for long-range queries, multi-node clusters with high availability and read replicas, and SSO with role-based access; a free At-Home licence allows two CPUs for non-commercial use. Managed options are InfluxDB Cloud Serverless (usage billing), Cloud Dedicated (single-tenant, custom price) and Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB. InfluxDB 1.x and 2.x are still MIT-licensed and still get releases, 1.13.1 and 2.9.1 in 2026.
strengths: The biggest ecosystem in the category: Telegraf’s 400+ plugins, client libraries, and a data source preinstalled in Grafana that speaks SQL, InfluxQL and Flux
Line protocol is simple and widely spoken, and InfluxDB 3 still accepts the 1.x and 2.x write APIs and InfluxQL, so existing agents and many dashboards keep working
InfluxDB 3 keeps data as Parquet on object storage, without the series-cardinality limits of the old index, in files other tools can read
Core is permissively licensed and starts as one binary with no dependencies, with a Python engine for downsampling, alerting and transforms
Many ways to run it: self-hosted Core or Enterprise, InfluxData’s Cloud Serverless or Dedicated, or Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB on your AWS bill
limits: Core is for recent data: with no compactor, a query reads at most 432 Parquet files by default (about 72 hours); raising the limit costs memory and object-store requests, and long-range history is an Enterprise feature

Three generations, three engines: Flux (2.x) is in maintenance mode and absent from InfluxDB 3, TSM data must be migrated, and since 15 September 2026 the Docker `latest` tag points to InfluxDB 3 Core, so unpinned 1.x or 2.x containers can jump versions
Clustering and high availability have been closed source since 2016; InfluxDB 3 Enterprise is priced per CPU core by quote, and the free At-Home licence is limited to two CPUs and non-commercial use
The 2023 plan promised a free InfluxDB 3 “Community” edition with a compactor; what shipped in 2025 was Core without one, plus the non-commercial At-Home tier
Cloud Serverless bills on four meters, including $0.09 per GB of data out, and has service quotas and no high availability

story: In 2011 Paul Dix and John Shahid worked at a fintech startup tracking hundreds of thousands of financial instruments, and found OpenTSDB and Graphite inadequate; Dix felt he had now solved the same time-series problem twice. Their next company, Errplane, went through Y Combinator’s Winter 2013 batch selling a monitoring service. At the Monitorama conference in 2013 they found validation not for a new monitoring product but for an idea they had long discussed, an open-source time-series database, and released InfluxDB that autumn.

Errplane renamed itself InfluxData in late 2015, the year the team replaced its storage layer with its own Time-Structured Merge Tree engine. In 2016 it moved clustering into the closed-source Enterprise edition, noting that fewer than half a percent of users ran clusters. 1.0 shipped in September 2016, and 2.0 in 2020 folded the rest of the TICK stack into one binary with a new language, Flux.

But the index behind every series grew with each new tag value, and memory-mapped files suited neither containers nor object storage. In November 2020 Dix announced IOx, a Rust rewrite on Arrow, DataFusion and Parquet. It became InfluxDB 3: first in InfluxData’s cloud, then, in April 2025, as the open-source Core and the commercial Enterprise.

choices.choice: No external dependencies and a SQL-like language
choices.why: The 2013 site promised a distributed database with no external dependencies, an HTTP API that JavaScript could call directly, and a SQL-like query language for time series, so developers could start without assembling a stack.

choices.choice: Its own storage engine, the TSM tree
choices.why: General-purpose engines weren’t built for time series. TSM borrowed the LSM pattern (a write-ahead log, read-only files, compactions) and compressed each column by type, using up to 98% less disk than the engine before it.

choices.choice: Clustering only in the paid edition
choices.why: Support contracts alone couldn’t fund development, and fewer than half a percent of users ran active clusters, so InfluxData kept the standalone server open and sold clustering and high availability.

choices.choice: Rebuild on Arrow, DataFusion and Parquet
choices.why: Every new tag value created a series that had to be indexed, so high-cardinality data could make the index bigger than the data. Columnar Parquet files on object storage removed that index and separated compute from storage; Rust gave finer control over runtime behaviour.
